title: Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve’s Law) Bill 2021
short_title: Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve’s Law) Bill 2021

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would legalise mitochondrial donation techniques in Australia under a national regulatory framework.

It would amend the Prohibition of Human Cloning for Reproduction Act 2002, the Research Involving Human Embryos Act 2002, the Research Involving Human Embryos Regulations 2017, an Excluded Goods Determination, and the Freedom of Information Act 1982.
The bill would allow women carrying mitochondrial mutations to have a biological child without inheriting those mutations, and would permit further research and training before broader clinical use.
changes: Legalise mitochondrial donation for research and human reproductive purposes.
Establish a national regulatory framework for the technology.
Allow women with mitochondrial disease risk to have a biological child without inheriting that risk.
Enable further research and training to build evidence and expertise.
Gather data on safety and efficacy before broader introduction.
Implement ethical safeguards identified through consultation.
summary.affected: Women whose mitochondria would predispose their children to severe mitochondrial disease, and their families.

There's a category of mitochondrial techniques which involve the transfer of material between eggs—namely, the maternal spindle transfer and the geminal vesicle transfer. They don't involve any destruction of an embryo in order to undertake those techniques. There are three other techniques that involve transfer of material between zygotes or embryos—namely, pronuclear transfer, first polar body transfer and second polar body transfer. These three techniques involve, necessarily as part of the undertaking of the procedure, the destruction of a zygote or an embryo.* > > *I note in passing that under the bill only two techniques—namely, maternal spindle transfer and pronuclear transfer—are permitted for the clinical trial licence phase. But one of these techniques—namely, pronuclear transfer—involves the destruction of the zygote or the embryo. Accordingly, these amendments, when taken together, would remove from the bill those techniques or procedures which result in the destruction of the embryo. speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to legalise mitochondrial donation in Australia through the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, named after five-year-old Maeve Hood from his electorate. The bill establishes a two-stage pathway—starting with lab research and a trial at one licensed clinic, then potential broader clinical use—to allow women at risk of passing on severe mitochondrial disease to have healthy biological children, with a free conscience vote granted across parties.

speeches.speaker: Mark Christopher Butler
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, arguing for a cautious, staged approach to allow maternal spindle transfer and pronuclear transfer techniques to prevent severe mitochondrial disease, which affects 2,000–5,000 Australians and causes one baby per week to be born with the often-fatal condition. He criticised the late release of government amendments but indicated he would personally support them, and noted the bill was a conscience vote named after Maeve Hood.

speeches.speaker: Julian Simmonds
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, arguing it would prevent about 60 Australian babies per year from severe mitochondrial disease by replacing the mother's mitochondrial DNA with donor DNA, and rejected claims that the procedure constitutes three-parent IVF or cloning. The bill includes a ten-year research and training phase.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: The speaker supported maternal spindle transfer research but opposed pronuclear transfer due to ethical concerns about creating and destroying embryos, and warned that limited egg supply could create commercial incentives with social consequences.

speeches.speaker: Jason Falinski
speeches.brief: The speaker announced support for the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, arguing it would maximise individual freedom by eliminating mitochondrial disease, which affects one in 200 Australians, and noted the United Kingdom's similar law has been positive over six years. He thanked Dr Doug Lingard and Professor Carolyn Sue for their guidance.

speeches.speaker: Mike Freelander
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, stating it offers hope to families with mitochondrial disease by allowing them to conceive genetically related children without passing on defective genes. He noted that about 50 to 60 children are born with severe mitochondrial disorders in Australia each year and thanked the Minister for Health, Mark Butler, Chris Bowen, Katie Allen, the Mito Foundation led by Sean Murray, and the National Health and Medical Research Council led by John Rasko.

speeches.speaker: Dave Sharma
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, which would legalise mitochondrial donation in Australia to prevent the inheritance of severe mitochondrial diseases, noting that around 120,000 Australians carry a mutation and about 56 children are born each year with severe forms, often dying within five years. The bill proposes a two-stage implementation: initially for research and a pilot program, then broader clinical use.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the passage of the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, which would allow mitochondrial donation IVF techniques to prevent children inheriting mitochondrial disease, and shared a personal story about her grandson Liam, who has the disease. She also noted that a fundraiser, the Bloody Long Walk, raised $175,000 for research.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, arguing it would allow women with hereditary mitochondrial disease to have healthy children, is consistent with existing Australian medical and ethical practices like IVF, and would be regulated by the Embryo Research Licensing Committee. They cited the case of Cooper Tierney, who died from Leigh syndrome at six months, and stated that mitochondrial donation is not germline genetic modification, as the UK parliament had determined.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Charles Laming
speeches.brief: The speaker strongly supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, which would allow a staged introduction of mitochondrial donation techniques in Australia, noting that about 60 children per year are affected by the severe form of mitochondrial disease and that the bill follows the UK's lead with a two-stage regulatory approach. They also acknowledged policy adviser Catherine McMahon for her work on the campaign.

speeches.speaker: Katie Allen
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, which would legalise mitochondrial donation in Australia to prevent severe mitochondrial disease, describing it as a safe, regulated technique distinct from 'three-parent IVF' and urging MPs to support the bill for the sake of affected families.

speeches.speaker: Zali Steggall
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, which allows mitochondrial donation techniques for research and reproductive purposes to prevent mitochondrial disease. The bill creates a two-stage implementation process over 10–12 years, and the speaker noted that about one in 5,000 Australians develop severe mitochondrial disease, with the bill named after eight-year-old Maeve, whose grandfather lives in Warringah.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Martin
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve’s Law) Bill 2021, arguing it gives hope and could save up to 60 babies a year by preventing mitochondrial disease, and highlighted the story of constituent Toni Catton and her daughter Alana, who died from the disease at age eight.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Keith Leigh
speeches.brief: The member for Fenner conducted deliberative democracy forums with randomly selected constituents on mitochondrial donation, and will vote in favour of the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021 based on the overwhelming support expressed in those forums.

speeches.speaker: Josh Burns
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, which allows IVF using a healthy donor egg to prevent mitochondrial disease affecting 120,000 Australians. He named Maeve, a five-year-old with the disease, and stated the bill gives parents the chance to have a healthy child.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, citing no reported live births from the UK in five years, unknown risks of altering the human genome, creation and destruction of embryos, and future genetic identity complications from three-parent DNA.

speeches.speaker: Matt Keogh
speeches.brief: The speaker argued against the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, citing risks of heritable genetic modification, insufficient safety data, and ethical concerns about creating three-parent embryos and destroying embryos. They noted that mitochondrial donation is banned in the US, has no confirmed live births in the UK since 2017, and is not permitted elsewhere, while safer alternatives like IVF, adoption, and fostering exist.

speeches.speaker: Peter Khalil
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, arguing for a staged, closely monitored legalisation of mitochondrial donation, citing annual healthcare savings of $33–66 million and the prevention of severe disease in 56 children a year, with a donor register allowing children to learn donor identity at age 18.

speeches.speaker: Anne Webster
speeches.brief: The Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021 was argued to prevent mitochondrial disease by allowing a regulated IVF process that replaces a mother's faulty mitochondria with a donor's healthy mitochondria, without creating designer babies or three-parent children. The bill is implemented in stages, initially for research and clinical trials, inspired by the UK model, and aims to help the approximately 56 Australian children born each year with severe mitochondrial disease, for which there is no cure.

speeches.speaker: Trevor Evans
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to allow a specific schedule for debating the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, including extended debate, member statements, and adjournment until 9:30 am on 1 December 2021, with deferred divisions.

speeches.speaker: Rob Mitchell
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve’s Law) Bill 2021, arguing that mitochondrial donation would prevent severe genetic disease while citing figures such as 1 in 200 Australians predisposed and 56 children born annually with severe forms. The speaker also highlighted the staged regulatory approach, privacy protections, and constituent Bethany Hodge’s hopes to have a healthy child.

speeches.speaker: Lucy Elizabeth Wicks
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021 but opposed the pronuclear transfer technique and a provision allowing sex selection of male embryos, and would support amendments to remove both.

speeches.speaker: Tanya Joan Plibersek
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, arguing that mitochondrial donation should be legal to prevent children from inheriting mitochondrial disease, which affects about one baby a week and currently has no cure.

speeches.speaker: Trent Zimmerman
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021, noting that 120,000 Australians carry a mitochondrial mutation and 56 children are born each year with potential for disease, and argued the bill provides hope for families through a cautious, staged approach.
